From a random walk to the Dirac propagator, in one space dimension

kimav80132 · 26 November 2026

A walker moves at the speed and flips at random at a rate . If what flips is its direction in space, the road to the Dirac equation needs an imaginary rate, put in by hand. If what flips is its time sense, the rate stays real: the quarter-turn that is usually written comes out of the calculation, and the same walk, summed over its zigzag paths, gives the propagator. This note goes through it in sixteen short steps. Every step is written on real counters. The formulas of usual quantum mechanics are quoted beside the steps, marked “usual symbols”.

  4. What Feynman’s rule needs. Steps 9 to 12 use the walk and nothing else. Step 14 uses one more fact: that the negative half is already filled, so that a walker cannot be added to it and one can only be taken out of it. That is the exclusion principle together with a choice of vacuum. On this page it is taken, not derived.

What is known, and what is different here.

That the telegraph process gives the Dirac equation only with an imaginary rate is the result of Gaveau, Jacobson, Kac and Schulman. That a walk which also runs backward in time avoids the imaginary rate is the thesis of McKeon and Ord. Ord and Mann then reached the real equations of step 6 from entwined pairs of paths (panel B): those equations are the first pair of their equations (6). That the Dirac propagator in one space dimension is a sum over zigzags is Feynman’s.

What is different here is the reading. The clock of the walk is , its two counters are ordinary probabilities, and no return path is used. The sign that makes the quarter-turn is not put into the construction. It appears at step 6, when the same two equations are read with as the clock.

Without . No is used in the steps of this page. It appears only in the lines marked “usual symbols”, as the usual name of . A real matrix on the four counters that commutes with is a complex matrix on , and that is the whole dictionary.

What is not claimed. This is one space dimension. It rederives known equations and does not predict a new number. One pair of counters alone describes a neutral particle. The second pair is what a charge needs, and what step 13 needs. Measurement is not discussed.

Checks. Every formula on this page was checked by computer: the step and its Taylor series symbolically, the walk and the sum over zigzags on a lattice, the count of zigzags with 1, 3, 5 and 7 corners, steps 8 and 11 to 15 on the four counters against the usual complex form, Feynman’s function against its closed forms, and the equations of step 6 against Ord and Mann’s.
